title: Mahatma Gandhi and the 'Scandal Times': 'I Have Kept the Most Valuable Part!'
summary: In Yerawada Jail, Gandhi's secretary Mahadev Desai handed him a vicious, insulting screed titled 'Scandal Times' sent by an opponent. Gandhi carefully unpinned the steel safety pin holding the sheets together, placed the pin in his box, and tossed the insulting pages into the wastebasket, remarking: 'I have kept the only valuable thing in this document!'
keywords: Mahatma Gandhi and the 'Scandal Times': 'I Have Kept the Most Valuable Part!'
full_text:
During his imprisonment in Yerawada Central Jail near Pune in 1932, Mahatma Gandhi spent hours each afternoon answering correspondence from across the globe. His faithful personal secretary, Mahadev Desai, sorted incoming postal packets.

One morning, Desai handed Gandhi a thick envelope containing several typed pages filled with vitriolic personal insults, scurrilous rumors, and hateful diatribes against the freedom movement, crudely titled 'Scandal Times.'

Desai was visibly fuming with anger:
"Bapu, look at the foul language this contemptible critic has written against you! It is filled with filthy slander. Shall we return it to the sender with a stern condemnation, or hand it to the jail authorities?"

Gandhi accepted the packet calmly. With patient fingers, he did not even read beyond the first few lines of spite.

Instead, Gandhi noticed that the five typed sheets were neatly fastened at the top corner by a sturdy, shining steel paper pin.

Slowly and deliberately, Gandhi pulled out the steel pin, opened his small wooden stationery box, and dropped the shiny pin into his compartment for reused fasteners. Then, with a gentle flick of his wrist, he dropped the abusive pages straight into the wicker wastepaper basket.

Mahadev Desai looked on, bewildered:
"Bapu, did you not even read his charges?"

Gandhi smiled peacefully:
"My dear Mahadev, why should I clutter my mind with someone's poisonous bile? Life is far too short to absorb malice. However, that gentleman was kind enough to send us a perfectly good steel pin, which will help us fasten our replies to poor weavers and villagers. I have kept the only valuable thing in his entire submission, and discarded the useless waste where it belongs!"

Desai's anger melted into reverence. Gandhi had demonstrated how a truly liberated soul remains totally untouched by hatred, extracting practical good even from those who wish him ill.
